extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science; professional scientists interested in the nature of scientific change and theory evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards used to judge, compare, and persuade scientists about competing scientific paradigms (when and why a community adopts one paradigm over another). Emphasis on problem-solving, anomalies, prediction, aesthetics, social factors, and the limits of neutral verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative problem‑solving ability
rubrics_metrics.description: Which of two actual and competing theories fits the facts better; counting or comparing the number and character of problems each solves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text repeatedly treats problem‑solving as the primary appeal to scientists: e.g., Newton’s success in predicting astronomical observations, Kepler’s Rudolphine tables. Caveat: paradigms define different problems and standards, so simple counting can mislead; conversion is rarely just arithmetic of problems solved. Examples: Kepler, Newton, Lavoisier cited as cases where comparative problem‑solving mattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to resolve crisis‑provoking anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a candidate paradigm can legitimately claim to solve the problems that have led the old one into crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legitimately made, this claim is often the most effective. 'Crucial experiments' are recognized in advance in some cases. But Kuhn warns that many new candidates solve few crisis problems initially, and that not every anomaly justifies rejection — there must be persistent or severe failure in puzzle‑solving to evoke crisis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative precision and predictive accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which a paradigm provides strikingly better quantitative predictions than its rival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highly persuasive when present: examples given include the quantitative superiority of Kepler’s tables, Newton’s astronomical predictions, Planck’s radiation law, and the Bohr atom. Quantitative success can rapidly attract converts even if the new paradigm creates other problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel predictions / prediction of unsuspected phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The paradigm’s ability to predict phenomena that had been entirely unsuspected under the old paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly persuasive because such predictions weren't 'built into' the new theory: Copernicus suggesting planets like Earth and phases of Venus (later observed), Fresnel’s white spot (an unexpected consequence that persuaded opponents), Einstein’s account of Mercury’s perihelion. Novel predictions can compensate when the new paradigm initially fails to solve crisis problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of decisive or 'crucial' experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of experiments able to discriminate sharply between two paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such experiments (or discriminating observations) exist or can be developed, they are powerful persuaders. Examples: experimental demonstrations that tipped support toward a new paradigm are discussed (Fresnel/Poisson white spot, later experimental verifications like the Foucault pendulum). But often such decisive experiments arise only after a paradigm is being developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic appeal: simplicity, neatness, suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the new theory is 'neater', 'more suitable', or 'simpler' — aesthetic judgments that attract some scientists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less effective in the sciences than in mathematics but can be decisive for a few early adopters whose support is crucial to development. Examples: Einstein’s general relativity attracts many on aesthetic grounds; De Broglie and Copernicus initially had limited articulable appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise or fruitfulness for future research (future‑oriented evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision based on the paradigm’s promise to guide future research and solve many as‑yet unresolved problems, rather than solely on past achievement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption often requires faith in future success: early adopters embrace a paradigm despite limited problem‑solving record. Kuhn emphasizes that science chooses what will guide future work, so future promise and potential to generate a productive research program matter greatly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to generate a research tradition (post‑adoption productivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the paradigm can be developed and exploited in normal science — producing puzzles, experiments, instruments, articles, and texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A winning paradigm multiplies experiments, instruments, articles, and books; early competent supporters improve it and show what it is like to belong to the community guided by it. This faculty of creating a productive research program is a key practical standard for long‑term acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility and transformation of existing concepts and apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which a new paradigm incorporates existing vocabulary, conceptual apparatus, and manipulative techniques — and reassigns or reshapes their meanings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New paradigms commonly borrow tools and terms but rarely use them in the same way; within the new paradigm old terms fall into new relationships. This leads to misunderstandings between proponents of competing paradigms and complicates direct evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incommensurability of standards and problem lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that proponents of different paradigms often disagree about what problems need solving and what counts as a solution (different standards or definitions of science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because standards differ, direct comparison is impeded: e.g., disputes over whether a theory should explain causes of attractive forces or merely note their existence. Incommensurability means paradigms can 'talk through' one another and that counts of solved problems may not be comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold/degree of falsification required to reject a theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every failure to fit data warrants rejection; there must be criteria of 'improbability' or 'degree of falsification' to justify rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn critiques Popper: if every failure justified rejection, no theory would survive. Popperians therefore need a notion of severity of failure; developing such a criterion encounters the same difficulties as probabilistic verification theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm‑laden nature of observation and impossibility of a neutral language
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations and any attempted enumeration of alternative tests or theories must proceed from within particular paradigms because no empirically neutral observation‑language exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probabilistic verification approaches that require imagining all possible tests or rival theories are untenable since such constructions are paradigm‑dependent; verification functions like natural selection among actual historical alternatives, not among an objective space of all possible theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and personal persuasion factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Non‑epistemic factors (reputation of the innovator, nationality, personal temperament, age, generational turnover) influence conversion to new paradigms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn notes Darwin’s and Planck’s observations: conversion often occurs slowly, a new generation or the death of opponents matters. Reputation can change reception of work (Rayleigh anecdote). Some conversions are due to idiosyncratic, non‑scientific motives and aesthetic or autobiographical factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for initial competent advocates to develop the paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Early supporters who are competent will improve and explore the new paradigm and demonstrate what membership in the new community would be like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if initial motives are suspect, competent supporters develop the paradigm to the point hard‑headed arguments can be produced; without such development the paradigm will not attract the wider scientific community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification as competition among actual historical alternatives ('natural selection' metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification picks out the most viable among the actual alternatives in a particular historical situation rather than establishing absolute truth among all conceivable theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kuhn emphasizes that verification is comparative and historically bounded: asking whether the chosen alternative is the best among all conceivable ones is not useful because tools to answer it do not exist. This limits the scope of evaluative claims.
